content: The second edition of the Guidance for National Tuberculosis Programmes on the Management of Tuberculosis in Children was developed by the World Health Organization (WHO) to provide updated recommendations for managing tuberculosis (TB) in children. This edition builds upon the first edition, published in 2006, which led to the revision or creation of child TB management guidelines in many TB-endemic countries. However, new evidence and recommendations necessitated an update to the original guidance. This updated edition aims to assist national TB programs in revising their existing guidelines and standards for managing TB, particularly in children. It includes evidence-based recommendations to improve the care of children with TB and those living in households affected by TB. National and regional TB control programs are encouraged to adapt these recommendations to their local circumstances. Since 2006, there has been increased attention to the unique challenges of TB in children and its recognition as a significant global public health issue. While children with TB may not contribute significantly to community transmission, the disease is a major cause of morbidity and mortality among children and mothers. Following the publication of the 2006 guidance, many countries developed national policies and strategies to address childhood TB. However, practical implementation of these strategies has often been limited. The current challenge is to bridge the gap between policy and practice by scaling up childhood TB activities in endemic countries. This second edition introduces several important updates and additions compared to the first edition. These include separate chapters on topics previously covered only in annexes, such as the management of TB/HIV co-infection in children and drug-resistant TB in children. It also introduces new topics, such as the importance of integrated care, and includes considerations for managing TB in adolescents, recognizing their vulnerability and the lack of specific guidance for this age group in existing TB management guidelines. The preparation of this edition adhered to WHO's evidence-based guideline development process, which was not in place during the creation of the first edition. Current WHO recommendations, already published in TB and HIV management guidelines, are referenced in this document. Any changes to earlier recommendations, including updates to their strength or quality of evidence, are highlighted. There is an urgent need to address the lack of epidemiological data on TB in children, particularly in high-burden countries, and to study how children with TB differ from adults in their immunological and pathological responses. This knowledge is essential for developing and evaluating better tools for prevention, diagnosis, and treatment. Despite these gaps, much can already be done to reduce the burden of TB in children. The development of this guidance involved a Guidelines Development Group (referred to as the Panel), which included experts who contributed their time and expertise. The WHO Global TB Programme reviewed these declarations and found no conflicts. The Panel's deliberations were supported by resource persons who presented evidence but did not participate in formulating recommendations. The revision of this guidance was funded by the United States Agency for International Development (USAID) under the TB CARE I Collaborative Agreement. The contents of the document do not necessarily reflect the views of USAID or the United States Government. The writing committee, led by Dr. Stephen Graham, Dr. Malgosia Grzemska, and Dr. Suzanne Hill, finalized the document after review by the WHO Guidelines Review Committee. Technical advice on drug dosages was provided by Professor Peter Donald and Dr. Susan Abdel-Rahman. Feedback and support were also provided by WHO staff and the WHO Guidelines Review Committee. This guidance emphasizes the importance of addressing the specific needs of children and adolescents with TB, improving the implementation of national policies, and scaling up efforts to reduce the burden of TB in children globally.
